source: CARE Cambodia (Pailin), "TIP Training on Maize Production" / បទដ្ឋានអនុវត្ដបច្ចេកវិទ្យា ផលិតកម្មដំណំពូតក្របម, 2009. Funded by AusAID (ACIMA project), the European Union (Pailin Food Security Program), and ACIAR (CCPMP project).
text:
Corn must be dried promptly after shelling (removing kernels from the cob). For long-term storage, drying must continue until grain moisture reaches 13%. Storing corn while moisture is still high risks mold growth, rot, discoloration, and premature sprouting.

Whole-cob storage: if storing corn on the cob (with husk), it should be kept in a well-ventilated crib or shed with slatted walls that let wind pass through, and dried thoroughly to prevent moisture in the cob from transferring into the kernels and triggering sprouting. Some varieties cannot be stored on the cob for long periods because their husk deteriorates quickly, which then makes shelling more difficult.

Common farmer practice observed in Pailin: farmers commonly build cob-storage cribs from woven/slatted material in the field to hold harvested cobs; shelling is then done — by hand or by machine — closer to the time of sale.

Freshly harvested corn has high moisture content. Bagging shelled kernels right after milling, without adequate drying, risks heating, mold growth, off-odors, and disease in storage. Buyers commonly discount the price of grain based on its quality and moisture content. After shelling, farmers must confirm the grain is properly dry: for storage over an extended period, grain moisture should be at or below 13%. A grain moisture meter is needed to verify this precisely — the source includes photographs of moisture-testing devices that can also be used for other crops such as rice, soybean, and mung bean.
